source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners (ICLR 2024)
finding: Founding paper. One prompt tells the model to recall K relevant, distinct problems with solutions, then solve the target. No labels, no retrieval. Tested on GSM8K, MATH, Codeforces level-A 2023 problems and five BIG-Bench Hard tasks, with GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, PaLM 2-L and text-davinci models.
numbers: K=5 on GSM8K, K=3 on MATH and BBH, K=3 plus self-written knowledge on Codeforces. Temperature 0 for math and BBH; Codeforces temperature 0.7 with 10 samples (Acc@1, Acc@10).
quote: Recall three relevant and distinct problems. For each problem, describe it and explain the solution.
limits: Single-pass design; Google DeepMind and Stanford authors; BBH tasks have about 250 items each.
agent_relevance: This is the S3 variant: the agent writes its own related solved problems before solving. Cheap to add to one prompt (O7).

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners (ICLR 2024) - Table 1 math results
finding: Self-generated exemplars beat 0-shot, 0-shot CoT and 5-shot CoT on GSM8K and MATH for every base model listed.
limits: Gain on GPT-3.5 GSM8K over 5-shot CoT is 1.1 points; no seeds or confidence intervals reported; davinci used an in-context demo of how to generate exemplars.
agent_relevance: Gains are real but small on strong models; the largest gain over 5-shot CoT is on davinci-003 (+7.0).

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners (ICLR 2024) - Table 2 Codeforces
finding: On competitive programming, adding self-written knowledge (a tutorial on core algorithms) on top of exemplars gives more than exemplars alone.
numbers: GPT-3.5-turbo-16k Acc@1/Acc@10: 0-shot 8/24, 0-shot CoT 9/27, 3-shot CoT 11/27, exemplars 13/25, knowledge+exemplars 15/29. GPT-4: 16/30, 16/29, 17/31, 17/32, 19/37.
limits: Exemplars-only Acc@10 on GPT-3.5 (25) is below 3-shot CoT (27). Small test set; per-cell sample size not given in the text read.
agent_relevance: Write the principle before the analogue; knowledge first, then exemplars.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners (ICLR 2024) - Table 3 BBH
finding: On five BIG-Bench Hard tasks with GPT-3.5-turbo the method beats 0-shot CoT and is competitive with manual 3-shot CoT.
numbers: Rows 0-shot / 0-shot CoT / 3-shot CoT / ours: Word sorting 66.8/67.6/68.4/75.2; Logical deduction 30.0/35.2/36.4/41.6; Temporal sequences 40.4/44.8/58.0/57.6; Colored objects 50.4/61.6/62.0/68.0; Formal fallacies 53.6/55.6/55.6/58.8.
limits: Row mapping read from the HTML table; temporal sequences is a small loss against 3-shot CoT (57.6 vs 58.0).
agent_relevance: Works on logic and symbolic tasks, not only math.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners (ICLR 2024) - Tables 4 and 5, scale and K
finding: Self-generation needs a strong base model. Small models do better with retrieved or fixed labeled exemplars. Best K is 3 to 5; K=1 hurts.
numbers: GSM8K ours vs fixed 5-shot vs retrieved 5-shot: curie-001 2/2/3; davinci-001 9/10/11; davinci-002 48/43/47; davinci-003 61/54/57. K sweep on GPT-3.5 (GSM8K/MATH): K=1 76.1/34.8, K=2 77.0/36.7, K=3 77.5/37.3, K=4 77.3/37.0, K=5 77.8/37.1.
limits: Crossover falls between davinci-001 and davinci-002. K=3,4,5 differ by under 0.5 points.
agent_relevance: Gate the recall step on model strength. For a weak model, supply fixed exemplars instead.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners (ICLR 2024) - ablations: diversity, order, self-consistency
finding: Asking for distinct exemplars matters. Knowledge before exemplars beats knowledge after. Self-consistency stacks on top.
numbers: Diverse vs non-diverse exemplars: GSM8K 77.8 vs 75.9, MATH 37.3 vs 35.2. Knowledge before vs after exemplars, Codeforces GPT-3.5 Acc@1/10: 15/29 vs 14/27. Ours + self-consistency: GSM8K 85.3, MATH 46.0.
limits: GPT-3.5 only; 1 to 2 point differences with no variance estimates.
agent_relevance: Keep the 'distinct from each other' clause; sample several traces and vote.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners (ICLR 2024) - qualitative error analysis (Sec 6.6)
finding: Authors hand-checked 50 correct and 50 wrong GSM8K+MATH cases. Even among correct answers, 15 of 50 had irrelevant or wrong exemplars. Among wrong answers, 28 of 50 had relevant and correct exemplars yet the model still failed.
numbers: Correct group: 6 irrelevant, 9 relevant but wrong, 35 relevant and correct. Wrong group: 10 irrelevant, 12 relevant but wrong, 28 relevant and correct yet unsolved (12 generalization gap, 8 over-reliance on one exemplar, 8 other such as calculation).
limits: Manual annotation by the authors, no inter-rater check; 100 cases.
agent_relevance: Analogue errors are common and often harmless; the dangerous cases are over-reliance and a target harder than the analogue. Add a check that the analogue transfers.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners (ICLR 2024) - stated limitations
finding: More output tokens than 0-shot CoT; fails when the model lacks knowledge of related problems; prompt-sensitive.
numbers: Compared with few-shot CoT: fewer input tokens, more output tokens (exemplars become output).
quote: our approach is better suited for stronger or larger-scale LLMs.
limits: No cost numbers given.
agent_relevance: Budget the extra tokens; test with paraphrased instructions.

source: Qin et al. (2024/2025) Relevant or Random: Can LLMs Truly Perform Analogical Reasoning?
finding: Main challenge to the founding claim. With GPT-3.5-turbo (temperature 0), self-generated IRRELEVANT examples beat relevant ones on math. Relevance is not the driver.
numbers: 500 test items each from GSM8K and MATH, three seeds; all BBH items, three seeds. GSM8K/MATH/avg: Relevant 71.5/33.3/52.4; N/A 75.5/36.1/55.8; Random-same-type 75.1/36.3/55.7; Random-different-type 76.3/34.1/55.2; Random biology 75.3/34.6/54.9.
quote: self-generated random examples can surprisingly achieve comparable or even better performance
limits: Did not re-run Yasunaga's 0-shot and few-shot CoT baselines. Main table uses one model (GPT-3.5).
agent_relevance: Random biology problems gave about 4 points over relevant math problems on GSM8K. The recall step may act as a worked-example warm-up, not as analogy.

source: Qin et al. (2024/2025) Relevant or Random: Can LLMs Truly Perform Analogical Reasoning? - BBH split
finding: On BBH the original result holds: relevant examples had the best average, so the failure is specific to math.
numbers: Temporal/Logical deduction/Colored objects/Formal fallacies/Word sorting/Average: Relevant 60.0/51.2/76.7/51.2/76.9/63.2; N/A 57.5/45.3/75.5/53.3/77.7/61.9; Random-same 53.1/48.8/73.5/52.4/74.1/60.4; Random-diff 44.3/44.8/72.4/51.2/69.2/56.4; Random-bio 57.1/49.5/76.1/50.8/74.9/61.7.
limits: Relevant beats N/A by only 1.3 points on average and loses on formal fallacies and word sorting. Row-to-method mapping inferred from the averages and text.
agent_relevance: Task type decides whether recall helps. Test per task.

source: Qin et al. (2024/2025) Relevant or Random: Can LLMs Truly Perform Analogical Reasoning? - MATH by subject and difficulty
finding: The gap is not caused by one subject or level. Irrelevant beat relevant on 6 of 7 MATH subjects and at all five difficulty levels (per the paper's figure caption).
numbers: Relevant by subject: Precalculus 10.4, Intermediate Algebra 9.8, Algebra 51.8, Prealgebra 56.8, Probability 22.1, Geometry 24.2, Number theory 37.0. N/A: 9.1/15.7/55.5/61.0/28.7/25.8/34.2.
limits: Number theory is the exception. Cell sizes are small (500 items split seven ways).
agent_relevance: Do not assume a hard subject needs a closer analogue.

source: Qin et al. (2024/2025) Relevant or Random: Can LLMs Truly Perform Analogical Reasoning? - mechanism: accuracy of recalled examples
finding: Relevant examples are more similar to the query but less accurate. Accuracy of the recalled examples drives results, not relevance.
numbers: Cosine similarity to query (GSM8K/MATH/avg): Relevant 0.54/0.41/0.48; N/A 0.19/0.28/0.24; Oracle nearest train items 0.65/0.63/0.64; Random-bio 0.06/0.11/0.09. Hand-graded accuracy of 50 generated MATH examples: relevant 62%, N/A 72%, random-same 86%. Variant ICL on GSM8K relevant 71.2; with GPT-4 corrected answers 75.2; with random answers 70.0.
quote: the key factor influencing the performance on mathematical reasoning is the accuracy of self-generated examples rather than their relevance
limits: Only 50 examples graded per type. GPT-4 answers mean the calibration variant partly tests a stronger teacher.
agent_relevance: An analogy step needs a verify-the-analogue check: wrong worked examples poison the solve.

source: Qin et al. (2024/2025) Relevant or Random: Can LLMs Truly Perform Analogical Reasoning? - fixed verified exemplars and other models
finding: A fixed set of model-written, human-checked examples (no per-query recall) beats the per-query analogical prompt and is cheaper. The pattern repeats on open models and other tasks.
numbers: GSM8K/MATH/avg: ICL-math 75.7/36.8/56.3; ICL-bio 77.9/34.9/56.4 vs Relevant 52.4 avg. GSM8K Relevant vs ICL-math: Llama-2-70b-Chat 45.1 vs 55.5; Llama-3-8B-Instruct 69.5 vs 75.8; Llama-3.1-8B 74.8 vs 80.2; Qwen2.5-14B 86.5 vs 91.1. CSQA 70.8 vs 74.6, MBPP 58.2 vs 62.0, GPQA 31.6 vs 35.8. On Llama-3.1-8B GSM8K: Self-consistency 77.6, Auto-CoT 75.9, ICL-math 80.2.
limits: Authors' own proposed methods; manual verification of the fixed set; instruction-tuned models only.
agent_relevance: Evidence that correct exemplars beat relevant ones. The agent could keep a small verified library instead of recalling anew.

source: Kojima et al. (2022) Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Reasoners
finding: Baseline that analogical prompting tries to beat: 'Let's think step by step' lifts zero-shot accuracy sharply on large models.
numbers: text-davinci InstructGPT: MultiArith 17.7% to 78.7%, GSM8K 10.4% to 40.7%.
limits: Generic guidance only; no problem-specific content.
agent_relevance: The floor that any S3 recall step has to beat.

source: Wei et al. (2022) Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Hand-written few-shot reasoning chains, the other baseline. Fixed exemplars, not matched to each question.
numbers: PaLM 540B GSM8K: standard prompting 17.9% to chain of thought 56.9% (+39.0).
limits: Needs labeled exemplars per task; the same exemplars for all items.
agent_relevance: Analogical prompting is meant as a replacement for these fixed chains.

source: Zhang et al. (2022) Automatic Chain of Thought Prompting in Large Language Models
finding: Direct precedent and warning: similar demonstrations can mislead. Retrieving similar questions with model-written chains did worse than random ones.
numbers: MultiArith/GSM8K/AQuA: Zero-Shot-CoT 78.7/40.7/33.5; Manual-CoT 91.7/46.9/35.8; Random-Q-CoT 86.2/47.6/36.2; Retrieval-Q-CoT 82.8/48.0/39.7 (the GSM8K and AQuA numbers use gold annotated chains). Of 128 MultiArith items Zero-Shot-CoT got wrong, 46.9% stayed wrong with retrieved demos vs 25.8% with random demos.
limits: GPT-3 only. With gold chains similarity helps; the harm comes from wrong model-written chains.
agent_relevance: Same mechanism Qin et al. later found: similar but wrong demos copy the mistake. Argues for diversity and checking.

source: Kim et al. (2022) Self-Generated In-Context Learning (SG-ICL)
finding: Earliest direct ancestor: a small model writes its own demonstrations for text classification. Conditioning on the test input gives more relevant demos and better accuracy.
numbers: GPT-J 6B, four classification tasks. Cosine similarity of generated demo to input: class-only 0.0689 (SST-2) and 0.0735 (SST-5); input-and-class 0.3051 and 0.3098. One self-generated sample is worth about 0.6 gold training samples; 8 generated samples beat up to 5 gold samples.
limits: Classification only, 6B model, no reasoning chains.
agent_relevance: The idea predates 2023; a generated sample is worth less than a gold one.

source: Liu et al. (2022) Generated Knowledge Prompting for Commonsense Reasoning (ACL 2022)
finding: Model writes knowledge statements first, then answers with them. Ancestor of the 'knowledge before exemplars' step.
numbers: Zero-shot T5-11b: NumerSense 64.05 to 72.47, CSQA 39.89 to 47.26, QASC 44.89 to 55.00. Fine-tuned: CSQA2 70.2 to 73.03, QASC test 76.74 to 80.33. Random sentences barely helped; few-shot GPT-3 answering directly was 14 to 20 points below.
limits: Needs a second model call and a vote over several knowledge statements; multiple-choice commonsense.
agent_relevance: Writing relevant knowledge first helps; supports Yasunaga's order (knowledge first).

source: Sun et al. (2023) Recitation-Augmented Language Models (ICLR 2023)
finding: Related idea: the model recites passages from its own memory before answering a closed-book question.
numbers: PaLM-62B Natural Questions EM: direct 25.76 (5-shot), recite-and-answer 20-path 31.34 (64-shot). HotpotQA PaLM-62B 20.51 to 26.46 EM; Codex-002 28.32 to 37.11.
limits: Targets facts, not worked problems; uses multi-path voting.
agent_relevance: Recall from own memory can substitute for retrieval; recall several times and vote.

source: Chen et al. (2023) Self-ICL: Zero-Shot In-Context Learning with Self-Generated Demonstrations (EMNLP 2023)
finding: Concurrent method: the model writes pseudo-inputs, labels them, then uses them as demos. Tested on 23 multiple-choice BBH tasks with text-davinci-003.
numbers: Average over 23 tasks: zero-shot direct 50.81 vs Self-ICL 53.93 (+3.12); zero-shot CoT 53.22 vs Self-ICL+CoT 55.54 (+2.32); real 3-shot 55.49. Win-tie-lose: 18-0-5 vs direct, 16-2-5 vs CoT.
limits: Gains are small and uneven: Temporal Sequences fell 57.60 to 35.60 in the direct setting. Weaker models make invalid pseudo-inputs.
agent_relevance: Independent test: small average gain, large per-task variance. Keep a per-task fallback.

source: Min et al. (2022) Rethinking the Role of Demonstrations: What Makes In-Context Learning Work?
finding: Explains why wrong analogues can still help on label tasks: random labels in demos cost only 0 to 5 points. Format and input distribution matter more than label correctness.
numbers: Random vs gold labels across 12 models: drop 0 to 5 points absolute; 1.7 on average for multi-choice, 2.6 for classification.
limits: Label-only tasks with finite outputs. Qin et al. find correct answers DO matter in math, where the output space is unbounded.
agent_relevance: Boundary: for open-ended math, wrong worked solutions hurt; for label tasks less so.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction
finding: Sister method from the same lab: ask the model for the general principle first, then solve. Fits the finding that knowledge before exemplars is better.
numbers: PaLM-2L MMLU Physics 66.4 to 73.2 and Chemistry 70.9 to 81.8 with step-back; TimeQA +27, MuSiQue +7. GPT-4: Physics 69.4 baseline, 82.9 with CoT.
limits: On GPT-4 plain CoT (82.9 Physics) is as strong as step-back results in the rows I read; gains depend on the model.
agent_relevance: An abstraction step before the solve is a cheap partner to recall; both are S3 variants.

source: Yu, He and Ying (2024) Thought Propagation: An Analogical Approach to Complex Reasoning with LLMs (ICLR 2024)
finding: Different use of analogy: the model proposes and SOLVES analogous problems separately, then reuses their solutions to fix or replace its first answer. Compared with IO, CoT, ToT and BaG.
numbers: Shortest path (100 graphs) optimal rate, 0-shot: GPT-3.5 IO 0.33, CoT 0.26, ToT 0.22, TP 0.65; GPT-4 IO 0.78, TP 0.88; PaLM-2 IO 0.14, TP 0.36. Creative writing (100 items) GPT-4 coherence: CoT 6.927, ToT 7.684, TP 7.989; user preference TP 45% vs ToT 33%. ALFWorld (134 tasks): Reflexion 79.1% vs TP variants 83.68 to 94.78%.
limits: More model calls; ToT scored below IO on shortest path; mostly authors' own reimplemented baselines.
agent_relevance: Solving analogues first and then transferring gives larger gains than only writing them; a candidate O7 design with an explicit transfer step.

source: Webb, Holyoak and Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models (Nature Human Behaviour; arXiv 2212.09196)
finding: GPT-3 can use a source story to solve a target problem (Duncker radiation problem), as in Gick and Holyoak 1980. With distractor stories it lost the solution until prompted to consider earlier stories, as humans do.
numbers: Human comparison samples: matrix reasoning N=40, letter-string N=57, verbal analogies N=57, story analogies N=54. GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) matched or beat college students in most settings. Radiation problem: alone, it proposed injecting the source into the tumor; with the general story it found convergence; with two distractor stories it failed; told to consider previous stories it succeeded.
limits: The problem-solving test is qualitative, a few prompts on text-davinci-003.
agent_relevance: Mirrors the human need for a retrieval cue; an explicit instruction to look back at earlier material makes the model use it.

source: Gick and Holyoak (1980) Analogical problem solving, Cognitive Psychology 12:306-355 (original not opened; paradigm described in Webb et al.)
finding: Founding human study. Subjects given Duncker's radiation problem rarely find the convergence solution alone; after reading the fortress story they solve it more often, but many fail to notice the link unless hinted.
numbers: Percentages not verified this session; look up before citing (recalled values: about 10% alone, much higher after a hint).
limits: Numbers are unverified. Webb et al. confirm only the paradigm.
agent_relevance: Human bottleneck is noticing the analogue. Analogical prompting skips it by making the model recall the analogue itself.
